## Introduction to Nuclear and Particle Physics {.title-card}

::: {.subtitle}
KT1 · 2026 · Lecture 1
:::

What is matter made of, and how can we find out?

::: {.notes}
Audience: fifth-semester physics students. Use the films as observations to discuss. Four-vectors receive a notation-only preview; the two-body invariant-mass calculation belongs to Lecture 2.
:::






## Observing particles {.section-title}

::: {.subtitle}
01 · Tracks, matter and length scales
:::

## Particles are passing through the room {.cloud-chamber}

:::: {.cloud-layout}
::: {.cloud-video}

```{=html}
<video controls muted playsinline preload="none" aria-label="Particles are passing through the room">
<source data-src="https://dlmultimedia.esa.int/download/public/videos/2014/07/044/1407_044_AR_EN.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
```

:::

::: {.cloud-copy}

**Before we watch**

Air contains alcohol vapour above a cold plate.

Cooling makes the vapour **supersaturated**: ready to condense into liquid droplets.

A charged particle **ionizes** the gas — knocks electrons out of molecules.

The ions seed droplets: **the visible trail is the particle’s wake**.

:::
::::

::: {.credit}
ESA, *Cloud chamber: classroom demonstration*, VP03 (2014). [Original film and creator credit](https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Videos/2014/07/Cloud_chamber_-_classroom_demonstration_video_VP03). [CERN teaching resource](https://educational-resources.web.cern.ch/cloud-chamber).
:::

::: {.notes}
Explain the setup on this slide before starting playback. A medium is the material traversed, here air containing gas-phase alcohol. Supersaturated means more vapour than can remain at equilibrium at the local temperature. Condensation changes gas to liquid; ions provide nucleation centres in the sensitive layer above the cold plate. Side lighting reveals the droplets, not the particle itself. Ask students to watch the variety of trails and how they appear. Full original ESA film: 6 min 54 s; use its observation section or the teaching demonstration. Playback is manual.
:::


## Questions about the tracks

Why do some trails look thicker?

What might their visible length tell us?

Can the appearance time reveal the particle’s speed?

Why do some tracks bend or look irregular?

::: {.notes}
Let students propose explanations before discussing appearance time and scattering. A film alone is generally insufficient for unique particle identification. Leave length versus stopping range and detailed energy-loss mechanisms for later; material is preserved in deferred-length-and-range.md.
:::




## Appearance time and changes of direction

A relativistic particle crosses $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ in about $0.3\,\mathrm{ns}$.

A nanosecond is $10^{-9}\,\mathrm{s}$. A normal camera cannot follow that passage.

Droplet formation and persistence occur much later.

Irregular bends can result from **scattering**: collisions that change the particle’s momentum.

::: {.notes}
Use c≈3×10^8 m/s as a reference, not a speed assigned to every track. Slow alpha particles still pass much faster than visible droplet evolution. Multiple scattering especially deflects low-momentum particles. Smooth magnetic curvature requires a known applied field; do not infer a magnetic field merely from a bent trail. Drifting droplets can also distort an older track.
:::



## What do we mean by matter?

In everyday language, matter is the material in air, water, rocks and our bodies.

Ordinary matter consists of **atoms**: a nucleus and electrons.

A nucleus contains **protons** and **neutrons**.

Particle physics also studies radiation and particles that do not form ordinary atoms.

::: {.notes}
Use ordinary matter operationally. Avoid the definition “anything with mass”: massive gauge bosons exist, and radiation carries energy and momentum. Introduce proton charge +e, electron charge −e, neutron charge zero.
:::



## What is a length scale?

A **length scale** is a characteristic size or separation relevant to a question.

A metre describes a person. A micrometre describes many cells.

$$1\,\mu\mathrm{m}=10^{-6}\,\mathrm m,\qquad 1\,\mathrm{fm}=10^{-15}\,\mathrm m.$$

Each step down by a factor of ten reveals a different level of structure.

::: {.notes}
Distinguish an object’s size from an instrument’s resolution. A femtometre is also called a fermi. Sizes of quantum objects are characteristic distributions, not necessarily sharp surfaces.
:::



## Matter at different scales

| Object | Typical scale | What is inside? |
|---|---|---|
| Atom | $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$ | Electrons and a nucleus |
| Nucleus | $10^{-15}$–$10^{-14}\,\mathrm{m}$ | Protons and neutrons |
| Proton | About $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$ | Quarks and gluons |

An electron has no experimentally established internal structure.

::: {.notes}
Ask how these statements could be tested. Emphasize scattering evidence and the distinction between nuclear and particle physics. Sizes are orders of magnitude, not hard boundaries.
:::



## Elementary and composite

**Composite:** has constituents and internal structure. Examples: an atom, a nucleus, a proton.

**Elementary:** no internal constituents have been established experimentally. Examples: an electron and a quark.

“Elementary” does not mean “smallest imaginable” or “stable forever”.

**How can we test for structure too small to see with a light microscope?**

::: {.credit}
[CERN: compositeness](https://home.cern/science/physics/compositeness/)
:::

::: {.notes}
No claim that experiments prove structure absent at every possible scale. Introduce the Standard Model as the theory in which quarks and leptons are elementary. A particle is described by a quantum state; later the course will develop the field description.
:::



## Quantum tools {.section-title}

::: {.subtitle}
02 · Wavelength, spin and measurement
:::

## Wavelength and wave–particle duality

**To look inside atoms, we need a probe with a much shorter wavelength than visible light.**

The **wavelength** $\lambda$ is the distance between successive crests of a wave. It sets the scale of detail accessible to an ordinary microscope.

Electrons have wave properties too: many individual electron detections can build an **interference pattern**.

**Can we use an electron beam as a microscope?**

::: {.notes}
Connect directly to the preceding question about testing internal structure. Visible-light wavelengths are hundreds of nanometres, much larger than an atom. Ordinary far-field optical resolution is limited by wavelength and aperture; avoid an absolute claim covering near-field or super-resolution techniques. Recall electron double-slit interference verbally: localized detector hits build a wave-like distribution. A particle does not switch between a classical wave and a classical ball. Wavelength is a spatial phase scale, not particle diameter. The next slide answers how to shorten an electron's wavelength: increase its momentum.
:::


## Momentum sets the wavelength

$$\lambda=\frac{h}{p},\qquad \hbar=\frac{h}{2\pi}.$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\lambda$ | de Broglie wavelength, a length |
| $p$ | Magnitude of the particle’s momentum |
| $h$ | Planck’s constant |
| $\hbar$ | The reduced Planck constant |

**Greater electron momentum means a shorter wavelength — a probe for finer structure.**

::: {.notes}
h≈6.626×10^-34 J s. Momentum is a vector describing motion; p here is its magnitude. At low speed p≈mv, but this expression is not valid at relativistic speeds. These are recall relations, not a second blackboard derivation.
:::



## A concrete scattering experiment

Send an **electron beam** at a thin piece of material.

The electrons are the **probes**. The material, and the atoms or nuclei being studied, are the **target**.

Measure the electrons’ incoming and outgoing directions and momenta.

A change in motion tells us about the interaction.

::: {.notes}
Define a beam as many particles prepared to move in nearly the same direction. A target can be a foil, gas, or another beam; it need not be a stationary classical ball.
:::




## A quantum microscope

A wave cannot resolve details much smaller than its wavelength.

**Shorter wavelengths let us investigate smaller structures.**

Particles have wavelengths too: increasing their momentum shortens their de Broglie wavelength.

In a scattering experiment, the change in momentum also matters. We quantify this in Lecture 2.

::: {.notes}
Keep this qualitative today. The spatial-resolution estimate R ~ ħ/Q and the definition of momentum transfer have moved to Lecture 2; high beam momentum alone is insufficient at very small deflection.
:::


## Spin: intrinsic angular momentum

**Orbital angular momentum** describes motion around a point.

**Spin** is an intrinsic quantum property, present even without orbital motion.

Its quantum number is $s=0,\frac12,1,\frac32,\ldots$

An elementary electron has $s=\frac12$. It is not a tiny rotating sphere.

::: {.notes}
State that “intrinsic” means a property of the particle, independent of its orbital state. Spin has observable consequences in magnetic interactions and statistics.
:::



## Measuring one component of spin

Choose an axis, called $z$.

For a spin-$\frac12$ particle, a measurement of $S_z$ gives one of two results:

$$S_z=+\frac{\hbar}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad S_z=-\frac{\hbar}{2}.$$

$S_z$ is the spin component along that axis. $s$ labels the particle’s spin.

::: {.notes}
A Stern–Gerlach experiment with silver atoms provides the standard two-output demonstration; do not claim a free-electron beam is used in the textbook apparatus. The total spin magnitude is √[s(s+1)]ℏ, so sℏ is not its magnitude. Massless photon spin states require additional care and are not generalized from this example.
:::

Rotate toward 90°: the mean z projection vanishes, but each result is still ±ℏ/2. Switch to j = 1, rotate to 90°, and compare the 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 distribution with the misconception that the state is definitely m = 0. At 180° only |j,−j⟩ remains. The blue arrow is ⟨J⟩, with length jℏ for these spin-coherent states, while the dashed reference radius is √[j(j+1)]ℏ. It is not an uncertainty orbit or a hidden vector of fixed direction. Axis tick labels are m in units of ℏ; the picture rescales when j changes. All amplitudes here are real and nonnegative for the active rotation exp(−iθJy/ℏ), 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, in the standard basis; amplitudes are complex in general. This represents a generic spin-j degree of freedom, not the polarization space of a massless photon. Formula and checks are documented in widgets/spin-rotation.md.
:::

## Fermions and bosons

| Class | Spin quantum number | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Fermions | Half-integer: $\frac12,\frac32,\ldots$ | Electron, quark, proton |
| Bosons | Integer: $0,1,2,\ldots$ | Photon, Higgs boson, pion |

Identical fermions cannot occupy the same complete one-particle quantum state.

Bosons can share a state. This distinction helps explain atoms and lasers.

::: {.notes}
State the Pauli exclusion principle carefully: electrons can occupy the same spatial orbital when their spin states differ. Classification by spin applies to composite particles too; not every boson is elementary or a force mediator.
:::



## Particles and interactions {.section-title}

::: {.subtitle}
03 · The Standard Model and its vertices
:::

## The four fundamental forces

| Force | A familiar manifestation | Particle-physics connection |
|---|---|---|
| Gravity | Falling objects and planetary orbits | Acts on energy and momentum |
| Electromagnetism | Light, electricity, magnets and chemistry | Charged particles and photons |
| Strong interaction | Atomic nuclei hold together | Quarks and gluons; nuclear binding |
| Weak interaction | Radioactive beta decay | Changes particle types; neutrinos |

**An interaction is the physical process through which a force acts.**

::: {.notes}
Use familiar observations first. Contact forces such as friction arise mainly from electromagnetic interactions and quantum mechanics. The residual nuclear force emerges from the underlying strong interaction. Gravity is not part of the Standard Model; no graviton has been observed. A force need not appear as a classical push: particle transformations are also interactions.
:::


## Charges and interactions

A **charge** specifies how a particle couples to an interaction field.

Electric charge couples to the electromagnetic field. Quarks also carry **color charge**, associated with the strong interaction.

**Gauge bosons** are quanta of the interaction fields: photon, gluons, W and Z.

::: {.notes}
Explain a field as a physical quantity assigned throughout space and time. “Color” names a quantum charge, not visible color. The field formalism and gauge symmetry will be developed later; do not require them today.
:::



## Matter particles and force fields

Quarks and leptons are the elementary **fermions** of the Standard Model.

The photon, gluons, W and Z are spin-1 **gauge bosons**.

The Higgs is a spin-0 **scalar boson**.

Particles can carry charge and take part in interactions, including some gauge bosons.

::: {.notes}
Use “fermions as sources, gauge bosons as mediators” as an initial organizing picture, not an exclusive classification. Gluons carry color, W bosons carry electric charge, and gauge bosons can interact among themselves. Higgs is not simply another force carrier in the same category.
:::



## Quarks, leptons and generations

**Quarks** carry color charge and participate in the strong interaction.

**Leptons** carry no color charge. The electron and neutrinos are examples.

A **generation** groups related quarks and leptons with the same pattern of interaction charges.

Ordinary atoms use up and down quarks and electrons. The full table contains three generations.

::: {.notes}
Neutrinos are electrically neutral leptons, while charged leptons are e, μ and τ. Generations are not successive layers inside a particle. Flavor names a particle type, such as up, strange or electron. The neutrino flavor states mix during propagation.
:::

## Reading a reaction

$$\mu^-\longrightarrow e^-+\bar\nu_e+\nu_\mu$$

$\mu$ (“mu”): muon. $\nu$ (“nu”): neutrino. $\gamma$ (“gamma”): photon.

$e^-$ is an electron; $e^+$ is its antiparticle, the positron.

The arrow means **transforms into**: initial particles on the left, final particles on the right.

::: {.notes}
Read this aloud like a chemical reaction. For a single initial unstable particle, the transition is a decay. Greek symbols here label particle species, not unknown numbers. Subscripts e and μ distinguish neutrino flavors; a bar marks an antiparticle. Superscript signs denote electric charge. Unlike a chemical reaction, the elementary particle species can change.
:::



## Check: read the symbols

$$\gamma+\gamma\longrightarrow e^-+e^+$$

Which particles enter? Which particles leave?

What do the arrow and the superscript signs mean?

::: {.fragment}
Two photons produce an electron and a positron.  
The arrow gives the transition; $-$ and $+$ give the charge signs.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask students to answer before revealing the text. The plus signs between symbols separate particles; they are distinct from the superscript charge signs. Explain sufficient collision energy verbally. No energy-unit calculation in Lecture 1.
:::



## From particle blocks to interactions

<div class="interaction-blocks"><span class="source-block">Source particle<br>quark or lepton</span><span class="join">↔</span><span class="carrier-block">Gauge boson<br>interaction field</span><span class="join">↔</span><span class="source-block">Source particle<br>quark or lepton</span></div>

A particle's **charge** determines which fields it couples to.

The same particle can couple to several fields. Some carriers carry charge themselves.

::: {.notes}
Return to the widget: select electron, photon, quark and gluon. Reuse its blue quark / green lepton / amber carrier blocks. This is an organizing picture, not a classical relay mechanism. Gauge bosons can be sources too.
:::

## Perturbation theory and Feynman diagrams

**Perturbation theory:** approximate an amplitude by adding terms with increasing powers of the interaction strength.

An **amplitude** is a complex number whose absolute square gives a probability. A **Feynman diagram** represents a term in that amplitude.

A **line** represents a particle field; a **vertex** joins fields that the theory allows to interact.

**The theory supplies the allowed vertices and their weights.**

::: {.notes}
An amplitude is a complex probability amplitude, introduced more fully later. Sum amplitudes before taking the absolute square; diagrams are not alternative classical trajectories. Perturbation theory works when the expansion is controlled; low-energy strong interactions often need other methods. No coupling expansion calculation today.
:::

## Reading an interaction vertex

<div class="vertex-layout"><div>

Solid arrowed line: a **fermion**. Wavy line: a **photon, W or Z**. Curly line: a **gluon**.

The meeting point is a vertex. Here we draw incoming particles on the left, outgoing on the right.

Line arrows track fermion flow; an **antifermion** arrow points opposite to its direction of travel.

</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Electron enters a vertex; electron and photon leave."></div>

::: {.notes}
The reaction arrow in an equation and the arrows on fermion lines have different meanings. A vertex is a building block, not a photograph or by itself a physically possible free decay. A free on-shell electron cannot radiate a real photon in empty space while conserving energy and momentum; this vertex occurs within larger scattering diagrams.
:::

## Photon: electromagnetic interaction {.gauge-slide background-color="#fff0cc"}

<div class="vertex-layout"><div>

**Couples to:** Electric charge.

The photon itself has zero electric charge.

$e^- \longrightarrow e^-+\gamma$

Electron in; electron and photon out. The electron species and charge are unchanged.

</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Electron in; electron and photon out. The electron species and charge are unchanged."></div>

::: {.notes}
Use as a vertex within scattering, not an isolated free-electron decay. All electrically charged elementary fields couple to the photon; neutrinos have no direct tree-level photon vertex.
:::

## Gluons: strong interaction {.gauge-slide background-color="#d6eaf5"}

<div class="vertex-layout"><div>

**Couples to:** Color charge.

Gluons carry color charge; there are eight gluon states.

$q \longrightarrow q+g$

Quark in; quark and gluon out. Quark flavor stays the same; its color can change.

</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Quark in; quark and gluon out. Quark flavor stays the same; its color can change."></div>

::: {.notes}
q means any quark flavor. Color is a quantum label, not visible color. This is a perturbative vertex, not an isolated observable free-quark decay. The eight gluon states form the color octet.
:::

## W minus: charged weak interaction {.gauge-slide background-color="#e5dcf5"}

<div class="vertex-layout"><div>

**Couples to:** Weak isospin — a quantum label grouping weak partners, such as electron and neutrino.

The W⁻ carries electric charge −1 (in units of e).

$W^- \longrightarrow e^-+\bar\nu_e$

W⁻ in; electron and electron antineutrino out.

</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="W⁻ in; electron and electron antineutrino out."></div>

::: {.notes}
Weak isospin organizes fields into weak partners. W couples to left-chiral fermion fields and their antifermions; chirality is deferred. The bar means antiparticle; subscript e labels electron flavor. Charge check: −1 = −1 + 0. Other leptonic and quark channels exist.
:::

## W plus: charged weak interaction {.gauge-slide background-color="#e5dcf5"}

<div class="vertex-layout"><div>

**Couples to:** Weak isospin — a quantum label grouping weak partners, such as electron and neutrino.

The W⁺ carries electric charge +1 (in units of e).

$W^+ \longrightarrow e^++\nu_e$

W⁺ in; positron and electron neutrino out. W⁺ and W⁻ are antiparticles.

</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="W⁺ in; positron and electron neutrino out. W⁺ and W⁻ are antiparticles."></div>

::: {.notes}
Charge check: +1 = +1 + 0. Ask students to compare the fermion arrows with the preceding slide. W vertices also connect up-type and down-type quarks; quark mixing is deferred.
:::

## Z boson: neutral weak interaction {.gauge-slide background-color="#e5dcf5"}

<div class="vertex-layout"><div>

**Couples to:** Weak neutral coupling.

Set by weak isospin (the weak-partner label) and electric charge. The Z is electrically neutral.

$Z^0 \longrightarrow \nu_e+\bar\nu_e$

Z in; electron neutrino and antineutrino out. Even electrically neutral particles can interact.

</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Z in; electron neutrino and antineutrino out. Even electrically neutral particles can interact."></div>

::: {.notes}
The Z coupling depends on weak isospin T3 and electric charge Q, with different left- and right-chiral couplings. Do not equate weak charge with electric charge or a single universal number. Z also decays to charged leptons and quarks. Flavor-diagonal neutral vertices here are tree-level examples; loop effects and neutrino mixing require care.
:::

## Carriers can interact with carriers {.gauge-slide background-color="#d6eaf5"}

<div class="vertex-layout"><div>

Gluons carry **color charge**: the theory allows three-gluon and four-gluon vertices.

Shown: one gluon leg in, two gluon legs out.

Charged W bosons also couple to the photon: a $W^+W^-\gamma$ vertex is allowed.

There is no elementary three-photon vertex in the Standard Model.

</div><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Three curly gluon lines meet at one vertex."></div>

::: {.notes}
The three-gluon picture is a vertex within a process, not a claim about isolated free-gluon decays. Four-gluon and electroweak gauge self-interactions are not all drawn. No elementary three-photon vertex does not mean no photon-photon scattering: charged-particle loops generate it. Gravity is outside the Standard Model and Higgs is a scalar, not a gauge boson.
:::

## From quarks to nuclear matter {.section-title}

::: {.subtitle}
04 · Composite particles and the strong interaction
:::

## Hadrons: composite particles of quarks

**Hadrons** are composite particles governed by the strong interaction.

**Baryons:** conventional valence assignment $qqq$.  
Proton: $uud$. Neutron: $udd$.

**Mesons:** conventional valence assignment $q\bar q$.  
Positive pion: $\pi^+=u\bar d$.

A bar means **antiquark**: the corresponding antiparticle.

::: {.notes}
“Valence” specifies the net flavor quantum numbers; it is not the full quantum state. Gluons and sea quark–antiquark contributions matter. Antibaryons have three valence antiquarks. More general multiquark hadrons exist.
:::



## Two classifications, two questions

| Question | Classification | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Does it have constituents? | Elementary / composite | Electron / proton |
| What is its spin? | Fermion / boson | Proton / pion |

A proton is a **composite fermion**.

A pion is a **composite boson**.

A Higgs boson is an **elementary boson**.

::: {.notes}
Return briefly to the widget’s composite view. A hadron need not be a fermion, and a boson need not mediate a force. Ordinary mesons have integer spin and ordinary baryons half-integer spin.
:::



## What is inside a proton?

A. Three stationary quarks

B. Quarks, antiquarks and gluons in a quantum state

C. A proton-sized elementary particle

::: {.fragment}
**B.** $uud$ gives its valence-quark content. Most of its mass comes from strong-interaction dynamics.
:::

::: {.notes}
Audience vote on valence content. Do not repeat the original claim that everything beyond valence-quark masses is gluon binding energy: quark/gluon energy and QCD dynamics require a more careful account. The proton is composite, and confinement prevents isolated quarks in ordinary conditions.
:::



## Before the animation: nuclear matter

Ordinary nuclei contain bound protons and neutrons.

In sufficiently hot, dense matter, quarks and gluons are no longer confined inside individual hadrons.

This state is called **quark–gluon plasma**.

The animation is an illustration of a nuclear collision, not a microscope recording.

::: {.notes}
Explain plasma here as a state of strongly interacting matter. It is not a gas of noninteracting quarks. The nuclear force between nucleons is an emergent residual consequence of strong dynamics.
:::

<source data-src="https://github.com/MindaugasSarpis/slidev-videos/releases/download/videos-shared/qgp_formation.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

**What happens when nuclei collide at high energy?**

CGI illustration · Original creator of this collected clip remains unverified. [Original CERN animation alternative: Piotr Traczyk / CERN](https://videos.cern.ch/record/2301156).
:::

Play 33 seconds. Explicitly identify this as a CGI illustration, not a camera recording of quarks. Introduce quark–gluon plasma qualitatively and the connection between nuclear collisions and hot early-universe matter. Do not describe it as recreating the whole Big Bang.
:::



## Interactions leave different signatures

| Fundamental interaction | What we observe |
|---|---|
| Electromagnetic | Ionization trails and light |
| Strong | Bound nuclei and particles containing quarks |
| Weak | Beta decay, with an electron and an antineutrino |
| Gravity | Falling bodies and astronomical motion |

Gravity is negligible in the particle collisions discussed here.

::: {.notes}
Tie back to the four-force introduction. Explain that detector signatures are predominantly electromagnetic and strong effects; not every force is measured by the same instrument. The weak example is beta-minus decay, not every beta decay.
:::




## Particles can be created and can decay

$$\gamma\gamma\longrightarrow e^-e^+$$

$$\mu^-\longrightarrow e^-+\bar\nu_e+\nu_\mu$$

Energy, momentum and electric charge are conserved.
The total rest mass need not be conserved.

::: {.notes}
Point out antiparticle charge, equal particle/antiparticle mass, and sufficient available energy for pair creation. A decay is a transformation, not evidence that an elementary particle contained its decay products. No rate calculation today.
:::



## Amplitudes and probabilities

A quantum **amplitude** $\mathcal A$ is a complex number describing an alternative outcome.

The probability is obtained from its squared magnitude, $|\mathcal A|^2$.

When alternatives cannot be distinguished, add their amplitudes before squaring.

Their relative phase can increase or decrease the probability: **interference**.

::: {.notes}
Recall complex numbers and phases verbally. Scattering rates include flux and phase-space factors, so a scattering matrix element alone is not a normalized probability. This is a conceptual reminder, not another derivation.
:::



## Quantum mechanics still sets the rules

$$P\propto\left|\mathcal A_1+\mathcal A_2\right|^2$$

Indistinguishable alternatives can interfere.

A Feynman diagram represents a contribution to an amplitude.

::: {.notes}
Brief verbal recap of amplitudes, superposition and Born probabilities. The proportionality allows for phase space and normalization in scattering. Diagrams are not movies of measured trajectories. Leave the interference expansion, spin algebra and perturbation theory for later lectures.
:::



## Experiments and evidence {.section-title}

::: {.subtitle}
05 · Accelerators, detectors and collisions
:::

## Before the laboratory films

An **accelerator** uses electric fields to give particles energy. Magnets steer and focus the beam.

A **collider** brings two beams into collision.

A **detector** measures signals produced when outgoing particles interact with material.

::: {.notes}
The field changes described here distinguish acceleration from steering. Magnetic forces alone do no work on a point charge. A detector records many collisions to infer repeatable physics.
:::



## A laboratory for the smallest scales

<video controls muted playsinline preload="none" aria-label="A laboratory for the smallest scales">
<source data-src="https://github.com/MindaugasSarpis/slidev-videos/releases/download/videos-shared/cern_overview_short.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

**Why do tiny particles need such a large laboratory?**

::: {.credit}
Original creator of this collected aerial clip remains unverified.
:::

::: {.notes}
Play all 11 seconds. Explain acceleration, bending and focusing, followed by collision and detection. Higher collision energies permit heavier states; large momentum transfers probe smaller structure. Do not make this a tour of laboratory statistics.
:::



## A detector on a human scale

<video controls muted playsinline preload="none" aria-label="A detector on a human scale">
<source data-src="https://github.com/MindaugasSarpis/slidev-videos/releases/download/videos-shared/atlas_footage_2022_004_002.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

**Which measurements must this machine make?**

::: {.credit}
ATLAS / CERN · ATLAS-FOOTAGE-2022-004-002.
:::

::: {.notes}
Play 29 seconds. The source is 3:2 and should remain uncropped. Use the shaft descent to establish engineering scale, then discuss tracking, calorimetry and muon detection.
:::



## What the detector measures

**Tracking:** positions of charged-particle signals along a path. Curvature in a known magnetic field helps determine momentum.

**Calorimetry:** energy deposited in material. A **shower** is a cascade of secondary particles.

**Muon detectors:** outer instruments that identify particles penetrating much of the detector.

::: {.notes}
These methods combine probabilistic evidence. Neutral particles can still interact: photons make electromagnetic showers, neutrons can produce hadronic showers. Neutrinos generally escape.
:::



## Reading a collision

| Measured signature | A possible interpretation |
|---|---|
| Track and electromagnetic shower | Electron |
| Electromagnetic shower, no incoming charged track | Photon |
| Track continuing into outer muon detectors | Muon |
| Momentum imbalance transverse to the beams | Undetected particles, including neutrinos |

Particle identification combines evidence from several systems.

::: {.notes}
These are idealized signatures, not error-free labels. Include charged hadrons verbally: a track with hadronic interactions. Detector resolution, acceptance and inefficiency can also produce missing transverse momentum. Optional live event display: https://opendata.cern.ch/visualise/events/cms
:::



## Describing a collision {.section-title}

::: {.subtitle}
06 · Four-momentum, mass and open questions
:::

## Particle kinematics {.kinematics}

**Kinematics** describes energy and motion before and after an interaction.

It is basic material for this course.

Today: a first look at four-vectors and how to add them.  
Next lecture: units, transformations and the algebra in detail.

::: {.notes}
Only introduce notation today. No invariant-mass derivation or Lorentz-transformation calculation.
:::


## Four components in one object {.kinematics}

$$p=\begin{pmatrix}E\\p_x\\p_y\\p_z\end{pmatrix}$$

$E$: energy. $p_x,p_y,p_z$: momentum components along the $x,y,z$ axes.

For this preview, we use a convention with $c=1$.

::: {.notes}
Say that a four-vector is a four-component object whose components transform together when the observer changes. This is four-momentum: one energy and three spatial momentum components. With c explicit its first component is E/c; the unit convention is explained in Lecture 2. p here denotes the entire column, not the magnitude of three-momentum.
:::


## Mass from the four components {.kinematics}

$$m^2=E^2-p_x^2-p_y^2-p_z^2$$

$m$ is the particle’s rest mass.

Energy and momentum components depend on the observer; this combination does not.

::: {.notes}
The left side is m squared, not m. We are using c=1. Do not yet introduce index raising/lowering, a metric matrix or a general scalar product. Covariant/contravariant components and the metric belong to the next lecture.
:::


## Four-vectors add component by component {.kinematics}

$$p=p_1+p_2=\begin{pmatrix}
E_1+E_2\\p_{x,1}+p_{x,2}\\p_{y,1}+p_{y,2}\\p_{z,1}+p_{z,2}
\end{pmatrix}$$

The subscripts $1,2$ label the two particles. $p$ describes their combined system.

::: {.notes}
This is ordinary componentwise vector addition. Energy and the three momentum components each add. Keep this a notation introduction without calculating the system mass.
:::


## Mass is not additive {.kinematics}

$$p=p_1+p_2$$

$$m\ne m_1+m_2\qquad\text{in general}$$

The combined mass also depends on the particles’ relative motion.

We will calculate an example in Lecture 2.

::: {.notes}
The inequality is not universal: equality is possible when two free massive particles have no relative motion. The point is that summing four-momenta is the conservation rule, while summing rest masses generally is not. The system mass includes centre-of-momentum energy.
:::





## Open questions in particle physics

- **Dark matter:** what produces the unseen gravitational effects?
- **Matter and antimatter:** why did more matter survive?
- **Neutrinos:** where do their tiny masses come from?
- **Families and masses:** why three generations and this pattern of masses?
- **Higgs and gravity:** why such different interaction scales, and how does gravity fit into quantum physics?

**To understand these questions, we first need the basics: states, kinematics, interactions and measurements.**

::: {.notes}
These are motivations, not promises to solve the open problems in this course. Dark matter is inferred through gravitational evidence; its microscopic identity is unknown. Neutrino oscillations establish nonzero mass differences, not the mass-generation mechanism. The Higgs hierarchy and quantum gravity are distinct questions grouped here to keep the introductory list short. References: https://atlas-public.web.cern.ch/Updates/Feature/LFV-FCNC and https://home.cern/about/what-we-do/fundamental-research/ .
:::

## What would convince you?

A. One impressive event display

B. A repeatable signal with checked backgrounds and uncertainties

C. A beautiful theoretical picture

::: {.fragment}
**B.** A discovery connects a prediction to reproducible measurements.
:::

::: {.notes}
Final vote. Return to the opening cloud-chamber observation and distinguish raw signals, reconstructed quantities and theoretical interpretation.
:::

## Before you leave: a quick quiz

**Three minutes · Try without notes or AI · Explain your reasoning**

1. In a cloud chamber, what are we actually seeing: the particle or something it leaves behind?
2. A spin-½ state points along $x$. Measuring its spin along $z$: is the result zero, or $+\hbar/2$ or $-\hbar/2$? With what probabilities?
3. A neutrino has no electric charge. Does that mean it cannot interact? Name a mediator it couples to.
4. Two particles have four-momenta $p_1$ and $p_2$. What adds: their four-momenta, their rest masses, or both?

**Write down one question you still have. Bring it to your tutor.**

::: {.notes}
Allow three minutes of individual thought, then invite brief explanations. This is a formative exit quiz; no bonus points or submission process are implied.

1. We see liquid alcohol droplets forming around ions left by the particle. The visible trail develops after the particle has passed.
2. The outcomes are +ℏ/2 and −ℏ/2, each with probability 1/2. Zero is the expectation value, not an allowed individual result for spin 1/2. This is the state obtained by rotating |1/2,1/2⟩ through 90 degrees about y in the widget.
3. No. Neutrinos participate in weak interactions through W and Z bosons. Z is the simplest neutral-current example; the absence of electric charge does not imply the absence of all interaction couplings.
4. Four-momenta add component by component: p = p1 + p2. The system's invariant mass is generally not m1 + m2 because relative motion contributes to its centre-of-momentum energy. Equality is possible for free massive constituents with no relative motion.

Use the final student question to identify which foundations need revisiting in Lecture 2 or the tutorials.
:::
